en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga,
Chapter on Saṅghādisesa Offenses.
8. The Training Rule on Malicious Faults At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta had realized arhatship at the age of seven.
"Whatever can be attained by a disciple has all been attained by him.
There is nothing further for him to do, nor is there any need for him to repeat what has been done.
Then, while the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
“Indeed, when I was seven years old, I realized arhatship.
Whatever can be attained by a disciple has all been attained by me.
There is nothing further for me to do, nor is there any need for the accumulation of what has already been done.”
"What service might I perform for the Saṅgha?
Then it occurred to the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta:
"What if I were to arrange lodgings for the Saṅgha and assign meals?"
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta emerged from seclusion and approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta said this to the Blessed One:
"Here, Bhante, while I had gone into seclusion and was dwelling in private, this reflection arose in my mind:..."
"When I was seven years old, I realized arhatship. Whatever can be attained by a disciple has all been attained by me;
there is nothing further for me to do, nor is there any need to repeat what has been done.
What service, then, might I perform for the Saṅgha?"
“Then, venerable sir, it occurred to me:
‘What if I were to arrange lodgings for the Saṅgha and designate meals?
Venerable sir, I wish to arrange lodgings for the Saṅgha and designate meals.”
“Excellent, excellent, Dabba!
Therefore, Dabba, you should assign lodgings for the Saṅgha and designate the meals.
“So be it, Bhante,” the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this connection, having given a discourse on the Dhamma, addressed the bhikkhus:
“In that case, bhikkhus, let the Saṅgha appoint Dabba Mallaputta as the assigner of lodgings and the distributor of meals.
And, bhikkhus, he should be appointed in this way.”
First, Dabba Mallaputta should be requested.
Having requested him, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me.”
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha appoint the venerable Dabba Mallaputta as the assigner of lodgings and the distributor of meals.
This is the motion.
Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me.
The Saṅgha appoints the venerable Dabba Mallaputta as the assigner of lodgings and the distributor of meals.
Whichever venerable one approves of the appointment of the venerable Dabba Mallaputta as the assigner of lodgings and the distributor of meals, let him remain silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
“The venerable Dabba Mallaputta has been appointed by the Saṅgha as the assigner of lodgings and the distributor of meals.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent.
Thus do I understand this.”
And the venerable Dabba Mallaputta, having been appointed, assigned lodgings together for bhikkhus of like standing.
For those bhikkhus who were experts in the Suttas, he assigned lodgings together, thinking:
"They will recite the Suttas together."
He assigns lodgings together for those monks who are experts in the Vinaya, thinking:
"They will resolve matters of the Vinaya among themselves.
He assigns lodgings together for those monks who are preachers of the Dhamma—
“They will discuss the Dhamma with one another.
He assigns lodgings together for those monks who are meditators, thinking:
“They will not disturb one another.”
To those monks who were given to frivolous talk and who lived with much physical rigidity, he assigned lodgings all together,
thinking, "In this way, these venerable ones will pass their time.
And to those monks who arrived at an improper time, he would enter the fire-element and assign them lodgings by that very light.
Moreover, monks would intentionally arrive at the wrong time,
thinking, "We shall see the miracle of psychic power performed by the venerable Dabba Mallaputta.
Having approached the venerable Dabba Mallaputta, they spoke to him thus:
“Friend Dabba, please assign us lodgings.
The Venerable Dabba Mallaputta replied to them, “Where do you wish for them, venerable sirs? Where shall I assign them?”
Intentionally, they made excuses from afar:
"Friend Dabba, assign lodgings for us on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Friend, assign lodgings for us at the Robbers' Cliff."
"Friend, prepare a lodging for us on the Black Rock on the slope of Isigili.
Friend, prepare a lodging for us in the Sattapaṇṇi Cave on the slope of Vebhāra.
Friend, prepare a lodging for us at the Sappasoṇḍika Cave in the Cool Grove."
"Friend, please prepare lodgings for us at Gotamaka Cave.
Friend, please prepare lodgings for us at Tinduka Cave.
Friend, please prepare lodgings for us at Tapoda Cave."
“Friend, prepare lodgings for us in the Tapodārāma.
Friend, prepare lodgings for us in Jīvakambavana.
Friend, prepare lodgings for us in the Migadāya deer park at Maddakucchi.”
The Venerable Dabba Mallaputta entered the fire-element attainment and went ahead of them with his finger blazing.
They followed behind the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta by that very light.
The Venerable Dabba Mallaputta assigned lodgings to them in this way:

“This is a bed, this is a bench, this is a mattress, this is a pillow, this is the place for excrement, this is the place for urine, this is drinking water, this is water for washing, this is a walking stick, this is the Sangha’s agreement on the rules; one should enter at this time, and one should depart at this time.
Having thus assigned the lodgings to them, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta would return once again to the Veḷuvana.
Now at that time, the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka were junior and of little merit;
consequently, they received the inferior dwellings and the inferior meals belonging to the Saṅgha.
At that time, however, the people in Rājagaha desired to give specially prepared almsfood to the elder monks, including ghee, oil, and additional curry.
But to the monks from Mettiya and Bhūmajja they gave ordinary food: broken rice with husks and sour gruel as the second course.
After returning from their alms round following the meal, they asked the elder monks:
"Friends, what did you have in the dining hall? Friends, what did you have in the dining hall?"
Some elders spoke thus:
"Friends, we had ghee, we had oil, and we had supplementary food.
But the Mettiya-Bhūmajaka monks spoke thus:
“Friends, we have had nothing; it was just ordinary food as we usually get—boiled grain with sour gruel as the second course.
Now at that time, a householder who provided fine meals was giving a regular meal of four dishes to the Saṅgha.
He would attend upon them in the dining hall along with his wife and children and serve the food.
Some asked for rice; some asked for soup; some asked for oil; some asked for additional curry.
Now at that time, a meal for the following day had been assigned to the Mettiya- and Bhūmajaka monks by the householder Kalyāṇabhattika.
Then the householder Kalyāṇabhattika went to the monastery on some business.
So he approached the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta; having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta and sat down to one side.
As the householder Kalyāṇabhattika was sitting there, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma.

Then the householder Kalyāṇabhattika, having been instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta with a discourse on the Dhamma, said this to the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta:
"Venerable sir, for whom has the meal for tomorrow been designated at our house?
"Householder, the meal for tomorrow has been designated at your house for the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka."
Then the householder Kalyāṇabhattika became displeased, thinking,
"How can these wicked bhikkhus eat in our house?
Having gone home, he commanded his female slave:
“Whichever patrons come, dear sir, have a seat prepared at the gateway and serve them with broken rice accompanied by sour gruel.
“Very well, noble sir,” that slave girl replied to the householder Kalyāṇabhattika.
Then the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka—
“Friends, yesterday we were assigned the meal of the householder Kalyāṇabhattika.
Tomorrow the householder Kalyāṇabhattika, together with his sons and wives, will attend upon us and serve us;
some will ask for rice, some will ask for soup, some will ask for oil, and others will ask for additional side dishes.”
Because of that very joy, they did not sleep at all during the night.
Then, in the morning, the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka dressed, took their bowls and robes, and went to the residence of the householder Kalyāṇabhattika.
When the slave girl saw the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka coming from afar, she prepared a seat at the gateway and said this to the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka:
“Sit down, venerable sirs.
Then it occurred to the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka:
“Without a doubt, the meal has not yet been prepared, since we are being asked to sit at the gateway.”
Then that female slave approached with broken rice and sour gruel, saying,
"Eat, venerable sirs.
"Sister, we are those who receive a regular meal," he replied.
“I know, venerable ladies, that you are those who receive a regular meal.
However, yesterday I was instructed by the householder: ‘Friends, tomorrow when those who receive a regular meal arrive, prepare seats at the gateway and serve them broken rice with sour gruel.
Please eat, venerable sirs.”
Then the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka thought:
“Friends, yesterday the householder Kalyāṇabhattika went to the monastery in the presence of Dabba Mallaputta.
Without a doubt, we must have been exposed by Dabba Mallaputta in the presence of that householder.”
Because of that very dejection, they did not eat their food.
Then, after the meal, when they had returned from the alms round, the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka went to the monastery;
having put away their bowls and robes, they sat down outside the monastery gate, cross-legged with their upper robes folded over their knees, in silence.
They were abashed, with shoulders slumped, heads bowed, brooding, and speechless.
Then the bhikkhunī Mettiyā approached the bhikkhus of the Mettiya-Bhūmajaka clan; having approached, she said this to the bhikkhus of the Mettiya-Bhūmajaka clan:
“I pay homage to you, venerable sirs.”
When this was said, the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka did not speak to her.
A second time...
[and] a third time, the nun Mettiyā said this to the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka:
“I pay homage, venerable sirs.
A third time, the Mettiya- and Bhūmajaka monks did not speak with him.
“What offense have I committed against you, venerable sirs?”
“Why, noble lady, do you not speak to me?
“Sister, it is because you look on with indifference while we are being harassed by Dabba Mallaputta.
“What can I do, noble ladies?”
“If you so desire, sister, the Blessed One could have Dabba Mallaputta expelled this very day.
“What can I do, noble ladies? What am I capable of doing?
“Come, sister, approach the Blessed One; having approached him, speak to the Blessed One thus:”
“Venerable sir, this is neither fitting nor appropriate:
that which was a direction free from fear, calamity, and distress has now become a direction full of fear, calamity, and distress;
where there was no wind, there is now wind.”
“I think the water is on fire!
I have been defiled by Master Dabba Mallaputta.

“Very well, noble lady,” the bhikkhunī Mettiyā replied to the bhikkhus Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, and she approached the Blessed One. Having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the bhikkhunī Mettiyā said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, this is neither well-covered nor fitting.
That quarter which, venerable sir, was free from fear, free from calamity, and free from distress—that quarter has now become fearful, beset by calamity, and afflicted with distress.”
"Where there was no wind, there is now a wind;
I think the water is on fire!
I have been defiled by the noble Dabba Mallaputta."
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this context, having assembled the community of monks, questioned the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta:
“Dabba, do you recall doing such a thing as this nun has said?
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One know me as I am.”
A second time, and a third time, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta:
“Do you remember, Dabba, doing such a thing as this nun has described?”
“As the Blessed One knows me, venerable sir.
“Dabba, those who are truly worthy do not evade in this way.
If it was done by you, say, ‘It was done by me.’”
“If you have not done it, say that you have not done it.
“Venerable sir, since I was born, I do not recall ever having engaged in sexual intercourse even in a dream, much less while awake.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“In that case, monks, expel the nun Mettiyā and investigate these monks.
Having said this, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
Then those bhikkhus expelled the bhikkhunī Mettiyā.
Thereupon the bhikkhus from Mettiyā and Bhūmajja said this to those bhikkhus:
"Friends, do not expel the bhikkhunī Mettiyā."
"She has committed no offense at all.
She was incited by us, who were angry and displeased, with the intention of causing her to be dismissed.
"But, friends, have you not groundlessly charged the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta with an offense involving defeat?"
“Yes, friends,” they replied.
Then those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the bhikkhus Mettiya and Bhūmajaka so groundlessly charge the venerable Dabba Mallaputta with an offense entailing expulsion?”
Then those bhikkhus, having rebuked the Mettiya-Bhūmajaka bhikkhus in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. [The Buddha said:
“… Is it true, bhikkhus, that you have groundlessly charged Dabba Mallaputta with an offense entailing expulsion?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, groundlessly charge Dabba Mallaputta with an offense entailing expulsion?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whatever monk, out of malice, anger, or dissatisfaction, should groundlessly charge another monk with a *pārājika* offense, thinking, ‘Perhaps I might cause him to fall away from this holy life’;
and if, at a later time, whether he is questioned about it or not, that legal issue is found to be groundless and the monk admits his malice, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.”
"But whoever" means whoever such a person...
"a bhikkhu."
...pe... this is the meaning intended here by the term "bhikkhu.
A "bhikkhunī" is one other than a bhikkhu.
"Corrupt" means one who is full of hatred,
provoked, displeased, dissatisfied, with a wounded mind, and become callous. "Discontented" means...
On account of that anger, that hatred, that dissatisfaction, and that lack of delight, he becomes displeased.
What is called "groundless" means not seen, not heard, and not suspected.
"By means of an offense involving defeat (pārājika)" means by one of the four [pārājikas].
"Should revile" means:
He either reproaches him or causes him to be reproached, thinking:
"Perhaps I might cause him to fall away from this holy life;

I might cause him to fall away from the state of a monk, I might cause him to fall away from the duties of a recluse, I might cause him to fall away from the aggregate of virtue, and I might cause him to fall away from the qualities of asceticism."
"Then at a later time" means when that moment,
that instant, that second has passed since he was charged.
"While being investigated" means...
When he is being interrogated regarding that very matter on account of which he has been accused;
"not being interrogated" means not being spoken to by anyone.

"Legal issue" (adhikaraṇa) refers to the four legal issues: the legal issue of dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa), the legal issue of accusation (anuvādādhikaraṇa), the legal issue of offense (āpattādhikaraṇa), and the legal issue of business (kiccādhikaraṇa).
"And the bhikkhu maintains a grudge" means...
"Empty was what I said; false was what I said; untruthful was what I said; it was spoken by me without knowing.
It is a *saṅghādisesa*...
...therefore it is called a *saṅghādisesa*.
One who has not seen [the offense] commits an offense entailing defeat. If he accuses him, saying:
"I have seen you; you have committed an offense entailing defeat;
you are no longer a monastic, you are no longer a son of the Sakyan," [he is guilty of an offense].
If he says, "There is no Uposatha, nor Pavāraṇā, nor any formal act of the Saṅgha with you," there is an offense of Saṅghādisesa for every word spoken.
It occurs even if it was not heard.
“He has committed an offense entailing expulsion. If he then accuses him:
“I have heard that you have committed an offense entailing expulsion;
you are no longer a samaṇa, you are no longer a follower of the Sakyan.”
“There is no Uposatha, nor Pavāraṇā, nor any formal act of the Saṅgha with you,” there is an offense of Saṅghādisesa for every word spoken.
It is so even when he is not suspected [of being a schismatic].
“He has committed an offense entailing expulsion. If he then accuses him:
“I suspect you have committed an offense entailing expulsion;
you are no longer a samaṇa, you are no longer a follower of the Sakyan.”
“There is no Uposatha, nor Pavāraṇā, nor any formal act of the Saṅgha with you,” if he says this,
there is an offense of Saṅghādisesa for every statement.
It is an offense of immediate defeat (pārājika) for one who commits an unseen offense of defeat.
If he accuses him thus: “I have seen and heard that you have committed an offense entailing defeat;
you are no longer a recluse…” [as before] … there is an offense of wrong speech, and an offense entailing suspension for each statement.
He has not seen himself committing an offense entailing expulsion. If one accuses him, saying:
"I have seen you and suspect you; you have committed an offense entailing expulsion;
you are no longer a monastic... [and so forth].
There is an offense of wrong speech; by means of speech, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
It occurs when one has not seen [the act], yet another accuses them while they are committing a *pārājika* offense, saying:
"I have seen you, heard you, and suspected you; you have committed a *pārājika* offense."

“He has committed an offense entailing expulsion. If he then accuses him:
“I have heard it and I suspect it… [and so on] … I have heard it and I have seen it… [and so on]…”
I have heard of you and suspected you, and now I have seen it: you have committed an offense entailing defeat;
you are no longer a recluse...
[as before] ...there is an offense by speech, and for each speech there is an offense of formal meeting (saṅghādisesa).
He is not suspected of having committed an offense entailing defeat. If one then accuses him, saying:
"I suspect you; I have seen you... [and so forth]..."
"I suspect you have been heard of by me...
[and so on] ...I suspect you have been seen and heard of by me; you have committed an offense entailing expulsion;
you are no longer a recluse... [and so on].
There is an offense of wrong speech; by means of speech, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
It is when one has seen another committing an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).
If one then accuses him:
“I have heard that you have committed an offense entailing defeat;
you are no longer a monastic...
[as above] ...there is an offense for each utterance, and for each utterance there is an offense of formal meeting (saṅghādisesa).”
It is seen that he has committed an offense entailing expulsion.
If one then accuses him:
"I suspect you have committed an offense entailing expulsion... [and so forth]."
I have heard and suspected that you have committed an offense entailing defeat;
you are no longer a monastic...
[as above] ...there is an offense by speech, and by speech there is an offense of formal meeting (saṅghādisesa).
He has heard:
"He has committed an offense entailing expulsion.

A person is impure because he has committed one or another offense involving defeat (*pārājika*).
If one who perceives him as pure, having obtained his consent, speaks with the intention of causing him to fall [from the Saṅgha], there is an offense of *dukkaṭa* along with a *saṅghādisesa*.
If a person is impure, having committed some *pārājika* offense,
and one who perceives him as pure, having obtained his consent, speaks with the intention of causing him to fall, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
A person is impure, having committed one or another offense entailing defeat.

If one who considers another to be pure, having asked for permission, speaks with the intent to abuse, there is an offense of defamation (*omasavāda*).

A person is pure, having not committed any offense involving defeat.

If one who holds an impure view addresses another who is pure with the intent to abuse, after having asked for permission, there is an offense of verbal abuse (*omasavāda*).
A person is impure, having committed one of the offenses involving defeat (*pārājika*).

A person is impure, having committed one of the offenses involving defeat.
